s1.syndrome_frame: Acute abdominal pain with anemia and evidence of hepatic bleeding
salient_findings: Anemia with hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
Active bleeding from hypervascular liver lesions on CT
key_facts: 64-year-old white man
Admitted in March 2016
On therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal pre-shimmering
History of two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV
Biopsies in August 2015 showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
Hemodynamically stable on presentation
No weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
Normal α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels
Abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions
Angiographic embolization and conservative management resolved bleeding

differentials: Hepatic involvement in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
per_call: Hepatic involvement in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia

shortlist.label: Liver adenoma
shortlist.why_kept: Prior biopsies showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy

shortlist.label: Metastatic disease to the liver
shortlist.why_kept: Hypervascular lesions and history of bleeding

raw.rationale: Biopsies in August 2015 showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy, and the patient's presentation with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia due to bleeding from one of the hypervascular lesions is consistent with a complication of liver adenoma

rejected.label: Hepatocellular carcinoma
rejected.why: Normal α-fetoprotein levels and lack of typical features on imaging make this less likely

rejected.label: Hemangioma
rejected.why: Hemangiomas are typically not hypervascular on imaging and do not usually cause acute bleeding

rejected.label: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
rejected.why: This would be unlikely given the patient's lack of weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms and normal tumor markers

rejected.label: Metastatic disease to the liver
rejected.why: There is no mention of a primary malignancy, and the patient's presentation is more consistent with a benign liver lesion complication
